1#main: The law of a garment in which kilayim was lost. In it are 2 seifim. A wool garment in which a linen thread was lost, or a linen garment in which a wool thread was lost—he dyes it, for wool and linen do not take the same dye, and immediately it becomes apparent to him and he removes it; and if it is not apparent, behold it is permitted, lest it fell out and went away—for he examined and did not find it. (In what case is this said? With kilayim d'rabbanan; but with kilayim d'oraisa one does not rule leniently in their doubt (Tur).)
2#main: One who buys wool utensils from a gentile must examine them well, lest they be sewn with linen (and one who buys garments from a gentile must undo their sewing and sew them with cotton (Tur)). And even if the gentile speaks offhand that he sewed them with cotton, he is not believed. And in places where linen is more expensive than cotton, one may rely to permit. {Rama: And it is forbidden to tell a gentile to sew garments for him with cotton threads even though linen is more expensive, for it is easy to sew with linen than with cotton (Rashba siman 561). But if he gives him cotton threads, it is permitted, and we are not concerned for substitution, since one can ascertain the matter—that linen threads when lit extinguish quickly and cotton threads burn (as implied in Maggid Mishneh chapter 8 of Laws of Forbidden Mixtures). And so is the custom, even though some are stringent (the aforementioned Rashba). And an Israelite suspected of sewing kilayim—his law is like a gentile. Some are stringent that he should not sew a wool garment with white cotton lest they suspect it is linen, and therefore they dye the cotton (Maharil).}
